claims.evidence: This is a key experimental observation reported in the study.

claims.claim: The intermingling of normal and defective segments was not anticipated by previous models.
claims.source: This striking phenotype was not anticipated by previous models (Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007; Uriu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous models.

claims.claim: DAPT was administered at 4 hpf, a developmental stage before the oscillating genes of the segmentation clock were expressed.
claims.source: Throughout this study, we administered DAPT at 4 hpf, a developmental stage before the oscillating genes of the segmentation clock were expressed.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: A treatment duration of at least 5 hr was sufficient to obtain defects on both left and right sides of the embryo for subsequent resynchronization analysis.
claims.source: This was a treatment duration of at least 5 hr, sufficient to obtain defects on both left and right sides of the embryo for subsequent resynchronization analysis (Ozbudak and Lewis, 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The spatiotemporal pattern of somitogenesis was visualized after its completion by whole-mount in situ hybridization for the myotome segment boundary marker gene xirp2a in ~36 hpf embryos.
claims.source: A record of the resulting spatiotemporal pattern of somitogenesis was visualized after its completion by whole-mount in situ hybridization for the myotome segment boundary marker gene xirp2a (xin actin-binding repeat containing 2a) in ~36 hpf embryos, Figure 1B,C.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, illustrated in Figure 1B,C.

claims.claim: Examples of defects observed with DAPT treatment included fragmented, mis-spaced, or mis-aligned boundaries.
claims.source: Examples of defects observed with DAPT treatment included fragmented, mis-spaced, or mis-aligned boundaries, Figure 1D–F.
claims.evidence: This is a description of experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 1D-F.

claims.claim: The anterior limit of defects (ALD) is given by the first segment along the embryo's axis that shows a defective boundary.
claims.source: As described in the introduction, the location of the transition from normal to defective segments resulting from desynchronization is termed the anterior limit of defects (ALD), given by the first segment along the embryo's axis that shows a defective boundary, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.
claims.evidence: This is a definition illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The first recovered segment (FRS) is the first segment along the axis after removing DAPT where resynchronization begins and normal segments form.
claims.source: After removing DAPT, resynchronization begins and normal segments form eventually. This transition has been recorded by the first recovered segment along the axis (FRS) (Liao et al., 2016) and then the posterior limit of defects (PLD), the most posterior segment along the axis with a boundary defect, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A (Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The posterior limit of defects (PLD) is the most posterior segment along the axis with a boundary defect.
claims.source: After removing DAPT, resynchronization begins and normal segments form eventually. This transition has been recorded by the first recovered segment along the axis (FRS) (Liao et al., 2016) and then the posterior limit of defects (PLD), the most posterior segment along the axis with a boundary defect, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A (Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: FRS and PLD label both an axial position and the developmental time of segment formation.
claims.source: Note that because segments form rhythmically and sequentially along the body axis, FRS and PLD label both an axial position and the developmental time of segment formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the sequential nature of segment formation.

claims.claim: In late washout experiments, a normal segment boundary sometimes formed shortly after ALD even when DAPT was still present, possibly due to desynchronization fluctuations.
claims.source: In late washout experiments, we observed that a normal segment boundary sometimes formed shortly after ALD even when DAPT was still present, possibly due to desynchronization fluctuations.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation with a speculative explanation.

claims.claim: The frequency of defects kept growing during an early phase in all conditions until reaching a plateau around segment 9.
claims.source: The frequency of defects kept growing during an early phase in all conditions until reaching a plateau around segment 9, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, suggesting that the desynchronization phase lasted until segment 9, at least.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: FRS is defined as the first recovered segment after segment 9, when the desynchronization phase was over.
claims.source: Hence, in this study we defined FRS as the first recovered segment after segment 9, when the desynchronization phase was over.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological definition based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: With late washout at 14 hpf (~9 somite-stage), several defective segment boundaries were formed after washout.
claims.source: We first analyzed the recovery of normal segments when DAPT was washed out at 14 hpf (twash-out = ~9 somite-stage (ss)), as in previous studies, Figure 1C. Several defective segment boundaries were formed after washout, suggesting that the level of synchrony was still lower than the critical value for normal segment formation during that time interval.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: With late washout at 14 hpf, embryos recovered a normal segment boundary after some time, indicating that the level of synchrony surpassed the threshold.
claims.source: However, embryos recovered a normal segment boundary after some time, indicating that the level of synchrony surpassed the threshold, Figure 1C.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: With late washout at 14 hpf, contiguous defective segments were often observed before FRS, suggesting that cells in the PSM were completely desynchronized by a DAPT pulse of this length.
claims.source: With this late washout time, we often observed contiguous defective segments before FRS, suggesting that cells in the PSM were completely desynchronized by a DAPT pulse of this length.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation with an inference about the state of synchrony.

claims.claim: With late washout at 14 hpf, PLD coincided closely with FRS, with the distribution of PLD – FRS peaking at lowest values.
claims.source: In addition, PLD coincided closely with FRS, with the distribution of PLD – FRS peaking at lowest values, Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,F, suggesting that once the level of synchrony surpassed the critical value Zc, it remained larger than Zc, as expected.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation illustrated in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,F.

claims.claim: The observation that PLD coincided closely with FRS with late washout can be interpreted to indicate that the level of synchrony increases monotonically over time, resulting in the formation of consecutive normal segments after the FRS.
claims.source: This observation can be interpreted using the desynchronization hypothesis to indicate that the level of synchrony increases monotonically over time, resulting in the formation of consecutive normal segments after the FRS, Figure 1A.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data based on the desynchronization hypothesis, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: When DAPT was washed out at 9.5 hpf (~0 ss), the majority of embryos had an interval along the axis where normal and defective segments were intermingled between FRS and PLD.
claims.source: Importantly, however, when we washed DAPT out at an earlier time twash-out = 9.5 hpf (~0 ss), the majority of embryos had an interval along the axis where normal and defective segments were intermingled between FRS and PLD, with the difference between PLD and FRS distributed more uniformly, Figure 1G,I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.
claims.evidence: This is a key experimental observation illustrated in Figure 1G,I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.

claims.claim: The intermingling of normal and defective segments suggests that the segmentation clock has a level of synchrony close to Zc in this intermingled region, and persistent fluctuations in synchrony level lead to intermittent defective boundary formation.
claims.source: This result suggests that the segmentation clock has a level of synchrony close to Zc in this intermingled region, and persistent fluctuations in synchrony level lead to intermittent defective boundary formation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data.

claims.claim: The physical model describes the PSM and tailbud as a U-shaped domain in a 3D space.
claims.source: The model describes the PSM and tailbud as a U-shaped domain in a 3D space, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods for details.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model, illustrated in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Cells in the model are represented as particles in the 3D space, subject to physical forces from other particles when they are closer than a typical length scale termed cell diameter.
claims.source: Cells are represented as particles in the 3D space, subject to physical forces from other particles when they are closer than a typical length scale that we term cell diameter.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model.

claims.claim: The model considers a spatial gradient of intrinsic cell mobility across the PSM and tailbud, with highest mobility in the posterior.
claims.source: In accordance with previous experimental studies, we consider the spatial gradient of intrinsic cell mobility across the PSM and tailbud, with highest mobility in the posterior, Figures 2B (Lawton et al., 2013; Mongera et al., 2018; Uriu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model based on previous experimental studies, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Axis extension is described in the model as cell advection from posterior to anterior.
claims.source: Axis extension as observed in the lab is described here, from the reference point of the posterior tip of the tailbud, as cell advection from posterior to anterior, Figures 2A,C (Jörg et al., 2015; Morelli et al., 2009; Ares et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model based on previous studies, illustrated in Figures 2A,C.

claims.claim: The model includes a left-right symmetric frequency profile along the anterior-posterior axis of the PSM to create kinematic phase waves.
claims.source: We also consider a left-right symmetric frequency profile along the anterior-posterior axis of the PSM, as observed in zebrafish embryos, to create kinematic phase waves (Figure 2D; Shih et al., 2015; Soroldoni et al., 2014; Jörg et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model based on observations in zebrafish embryos, illustrated in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The frequency of oscillation is highest at the tip of the tailbud and gradually decreases toward the anterior PSM.
claims.source: The frequency of oscillation is highest at the tip of the tailbud and gradually decreases toward the anterior PSM.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model.

claims.claim: When a simulation was started from a uniformly synchronized initial condition, the frequency profile generated left-right symmetrical kinematic phase waves due to growing phase differences between the anterior and posterior PSM.
claims.source: When a simulation was started from a uniformly synchronized initial condition, the frequency profile generated left-right symmetrical kinematic phase waves due to growing phase differences between the anterior and posterior PSM, Figure 2E and Figure 2—video 1.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 2E and Figure 2—video 1.

claims.claim: The oscillation is arrested when cells leave the PSM from its anterior end.
claims.source: To model the formed segments, we arrest the oscillation when cells leave the PSM from its anterior end xa, Figure 2A,E.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model, illustrated in Figure 2A,E.

claims.claim: The arrested phase stripes in the region x < xa are representative of segment boundaries.
claims.source: The arrested phase stripes in the region x < xa are representative of segment boundaries, and the segment length is the wavelength of this arrested phase pattern.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model.

claims.claim: New cells with random phase values are added at random positions in the PSM and tailbud to balance the cells exiting through the anterior end of the PSM.
claims.source: Consequently, we add new cells with random phase values (Horikawa et al., 2006) at random positions in the PSM and tailbud to balance the cells exiting through the anterior end of the PSM.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model based on a citation.

claims.claim: Resynchronization simulations were started with random initial phases assigned to cells, representing the state of the PSM and tailbud immediately after DAPT washout.
claims.source: As an initial condition, we described the state of the PSM and tailbud immediately after DAPT washout by assigning random initial phases to cells, top panel in Figure 3A, as an extended treatment of saturating dose of DAPT was expected to cause such complete randomization of oscillator phases (Delaune et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup based on a citation, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In the desynchronized state, normal segment boundaries – as defined by ordered phase stripes – did not form, matching the experimental appearance of embryos with persistent loss of Delta-Notch signaling.
claims.source: In this desynchronized state, normal segment boundaries – as defined by ordered phase stripes – did not form, matching the experimental appearance of embryos with persistent loss of Delta-Notch signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations that matches experimental observations.

claims.claim: The model qualitatively explains the formation of intermingled defective segments by the emergence of persistent phase vortices in the posterior PSM and their advection through the tissue to the anterior.
claims.source: The model qualitatively explains the formation of these intermingled defective segments by the emergence of persistent phase vortices in the posterior PSM and their advection through the tissue to the anterior.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the model.

claims.claim: Due to local coupling, cells first formed local phase synchronization.
claims.source: To characterize resynchronization dynamics, we computed local phase order at each position along the anterior-posterior axis, Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. Due to local coupling, cells first formed local phase synchronization, Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—video 1.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—video 1.

claims.claim: During the first stage of synchrony recovery, the kymograph of local phase order shows three locally synchronized domains that extended their size due to an increase in number of synchronized cells at the same time as they were advected in an anterior direction.
claims.source: During the first stage of this synchrony recovery, the kymograph of local phase order shows three locally synchronized domains that extended their size due to an increase in number of synchronized cells at the same time as they were advected in an anterior direction, Figure 3B,E.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3B,E.

claims.claim: When the size of the most anterior domain with local phase order above a threshold of 0.85 (Zc) exceeded one segment length at its arrival in the anterior end of the PSM, a first recovered segment (FRS) was formed in a simulation.
claims.source: When the size of the most anterior domain with local phase order above a threshold of 0.85 (Zc) exceeded one segment length at its arrival in the anterior end of the PSM, a first recovered segment (FRS) was formed in a simulation, blue triangles in Figure 3A,B,F.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3A,B,F.

claims.claim: Because local interactions drove resynchronization in a spatially heterogeneous manner, domains where phase order was lower than Zc could exist more posterior to such a well-synchronized domain.
claims.source: However, because local interactions drove resynchronization in a spatially heterogeneous manner, domains where phase order was lower than Zc could exist more posterior to such a well-synchronized domain, Figure 3B,E.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3B,E.

claims.claim: Subsequent arrival of the less synchronized domains caused fluctuation of the local order parameter in the anterior end of the PSM, which resulted in defective segment formation after FRS.
claims.source: Subsequent arrival of the less synchronized domains caused fluctuation of the local order parameter in the anterior end of the PSM, which resulted in defective segment formation after FRS, Figure 3A,F.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3A,F.

claims.claim: Patterns of synchronized domains in the left and right sides of the PSM were not well correlated during the time interval of intermingled defects.
claims.source: Note that patterns of synchronized domains in the left and right sides of the PSM were not well correlated during this time interval (Figure 3—video 1) despite a left-right symmetrical frequency profile.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3—video 1.

claims.claim: The numerical simulation suggests that a sequence of synchronized and less synchronized domains moving along the PSM results in an intermingling of normal and defective segments along the axis.
claims.source: Thus, the numerical simulation suggests that a sequence of synchronized and less synchronized domains moving along the PSM results in an intermingling of normal and defective segments along the axis. This intermingling matches the experimental observations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from simulations that matches experimental observations.

claims.claim: Less-synchronized domains typically formed persistent phase patterns that rotated along an axis as a vortex.
claims.source: These less-synchronized domains typically formed persistent phase patterns that rotated along an axis as a vortex, as illustrated in the simulation, Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1.

claims.claim: The kymograph of the vorticity indicates that the less synchronized domains in the kymograph of phase order were caused by the phase vortices.
claims.source: The kymograph of the vorticity indicates that the less synchronized domains in the kymograph of phase order were caused by the phase vortices, Figure 3A–C.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3A–C.

claims.claim: When a vortex was brought to the anterior end of the PSM through cell advection, it was converted into a defective segment boundary and delayed the PLD.
claims.source: When a vortex was brought to the anterior end of the PSM through cell advection, it was converted into a defective segment boundary and delayed the PLD, Figure 3B,C.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: The passage of each vortex into the anterior PSM in the simulations generated a segment defect with a characteristic length of one or two segments.
claims.source: The passage of each vortex into the anterior PSM in the simulations generated a segment defect with a characteristic length of one or two segments, Figure 3A–D,F.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3A–D,F.

claims.claim: The size distributions of defect lengths were in quantitative agreement between simulation and embryonic data across all embryonic stages and all simulations.
claims.source: We compared these defect lengths between simulation and embryonic data and found that across all embryonic stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and all simulations (see Figure 4, below), the size distributions were in quantitative agreement, Figure 3—figure supplement 3.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between simulation and experimental data, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The invariant length scale of the defect size is consistent with phase vortices as the origins of intermingled segment defects in the embryo.
claims.source: The resulting invariant length scale of the defect size is shown for simulation and embryonic data in Figure 3G,H. This finding is consistent with phase vortices as the origins of intermingled segment defects in the embryo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing simulation and experimental data, illustrated in Figure 3G,H.

claims.claim: The speed of cell mixing at the tailbud, PSM length L and the cell advection pattern in the PSM did not affect FRS, whereas they strongly affected PLD.
claims.source: We found that the speed of cell mixing at the tailbud, PSM length L and the cell advection pattern in the PSM did not affect FRS, whereas they strongly affected PLD, Figure 3—figure supplements 4–6.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplements 4–6.

claims.claim: Faster cell mixing in the tailbud reduced PLD because it prevented the formation of persistent phase vortices at the tailbud.
claims.source: Faster cell mixing in the tailbud reduced PLD, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, because it prevented the formation of persistent phase vortices at the tailbud.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations with an explanation, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Longer PSM increased PLD because a phase vortex needed more time to arrive at the anterior end by the cell advection.
claims.source: Longer PSM increased PLD because a phase vortex needed more time to arrive at the anterior end by the cell advection, Figure 3—figure supplement 5.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations with an explanation, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: If cell advection was slower at the posterior part of the PSM, PLD became larger because vortices stayed longer at the posterior part.
claims.source: If cell advection was slower at the posterior part of the PSM, PLD became larger because vortices stayed longer at the posterior part, Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations with an explanation, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claims.claim: If cell advection was faster at the posterior part, PLD became smaller due to faster transport of phase vortices to the anterior part.
claims.source: In contrast, if cell advection was faster at the posterior part, PLD became smaller due to faster transport of phase vortices to the anterior part, Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations with an explanation, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claims.claim: Smaller PSM radius r decreased FRS and PLD.
claims.source: Smaller PSM radius r decreased FRS and PLD, Figure 3—figure supplement 7.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: Smaller cell number at each position in the PSM with a smaller radius r allowed local coupling to more rapidly generate a synchronized domain as large as the tissue diameter, leading to a normal segment.
claims.source: Smaller cell number at each position in the PSM with a smaller radius r allowed local coupling to more rapidly generate a synchronized domain as large as the tissue diameter, leading to a normal segment.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the simulation result.

claims.claim: A larger coupling strength reduced the time for local order to form, including vortex patterns, and as a result, the last-formed vortex departed the posterior PSM earlier, decreasing PLD.
claims.source: A larger coupling strength reduced the time for local order to form, including vortex patterns. As a result, the last-formed vortex departed the posterior PSM earlier, decreasing PLD.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the simulation result.

claims.claim: In resynchronization simulations with coupling, both FRS and PLD only weakly depended on the noise intensity for biologically realistic values.
claims.source: However, in resynchronization simulations with coupling, both FRS and PLD only weakly depended on the noise intensity for biologically realistic values, Figure 3—figure supplement 9.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claims.claim: The shape of frequency profile and the torus size for the tailbud R did not influence either FRS or PLD.
claims.source: Finally, we found that the shape of frequency profile and the torus size for the tailbud R did not influence either FRS or PLD, Figure 3—figure supplements 10 and 11.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplements 10 and 11.

claims.claim: FRS was determined by parameters that influence local synchronization of oscillators.
claims.source: In summary, FRS was determined by parameters that influence local synchronization of oscillators.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claims.claim: PLD was influenced by parameters that control local synchronization, formation of phase vortices, and their arrival at the anterior end of the PSM.
claims.source: PLD, on the other hand, was influenced by parameters that control local synchronization, formation of phase vortices, and their arrival at the anterior end of the PSM.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claims.claim: PSM shortening decreased the time to PLD for later washout times because in a shorter PSM at later somite stages phase vortices reached the anterior end of the PSM more quickly.
claims.source: PSM shortening decreased the time to PLD for later washout times, Figure 4B, because in a shorter PSM at later somite stages phase vortices reached the anterior end of the PSM more quickly, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations with an explanation, illustrated in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: PSM shortening did not affect FRS.
claims.source: As expected from the independence of FRS on constant PSM length, PSM shortening did not affect FRS, Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: A change in advection pattern increased time to PLD for earlier DAPT washout.
claims.source: We found that such a change in advection pattern increased time to PLD for earlier DAPT washout, Figure 4C.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: When advection did not occur in the posterior PSM at earlier somite-stages, the movement of phase vortices relative to the tailbud was slowed in that region, delaying PLD for earlier washout timing.
claims.source: When advection did not occur in the posterior PSM at earlier somite-stages, the movement of phase vortices relative to the tailbud was slowed in that region, delaying PLD for earlier washout timing, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations with an explanation, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: A change in advection pattern did not affect FRS.
claims.source: As expected from the independence of FRS on constant advection patterns, a change in pattern did not affect FRS, Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–G.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations, illustrated in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–G.

claims.claim: Changes in tissue length and cell advection pattern observed in the embryo over developmental time may have an impact on resynchronization dynamics, reflecting in the decrease in difference between FRS and PLD.
claims.source: Taken together, these results predict that the changes in tissue length and cell advection pattern observed in the embryo over developmental time may have an impact on resynchronization dynamics, reflecting in the decrease in difference between FRS and PLD.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: FRS and PLD both increased with later washout times.
claims.source: We found that FRS and PLD both increased with later washout times, Figure 4—figure supplement 3.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The time to PLD (PLD – twash-out) decreased gradually over developmental time.
claims.source: In accordance with the prediction of the model, the time to PLD (PLD – twash-out) decreased gradually over developmental time, Figure 4E.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation that matches a model prediction, illustrated in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The experimentally observed gradual decrease in time to FRS (FRS – twash-out) was not expected from the simulations with PSM shortening and changing cell advection pattern alone.
claims.source: In contrast, the experimentally observed gradual decrease in time to FRS (FRS – twash-out) in Figure 4E was not expected from the simulations, Figure 4B,C.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and simulation results, illustrated in Figure 4E, 4B, and 4C.

claims.claim: After washout, it took ~13 segments to observe FRS for an earlier washout time, whereas it took eight segments for a later washout time.
claims.source: After washout, it took ~13 segments to observe FRS for an earlier washout time, whereas it took eight segments for a later washout time.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claims.claim: Embryos yielded more scattered, non-continuous defects with earlier than with later washouts.
claims.source: Embryos yielded more scattered, non-continuous defects with earlier than with later washouts, Figure 4D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–G.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation, illustrated in Figure 4D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–G.

claims.claim: FRS might be affected by mechanisms that determine the level of local synchronization.
claims.source: We therefore hypothesized that FRS might instead be affected by mechanisms that determine the level of local synchronization.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental observations.

claims.claim: An increase in coupling strength over developmental stages in the embryo could be caused by an increase in the abundance or activity of Delta and Notch proteins in cells, an increase in the contact surface area between neighboring cells, or some other mechanism.
claims.source: An increase in coupling strength over developmental stages in the embryo could be caused by an increase in the abundance or activity of Delta and Notch proteins in cells (Wright et al., 2011; Liao et al., 2016; Haddon et al., 1998; Westin and Lardelli, 1997), an increase in the contact surface area between neighboring cells, or some other mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about possible mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A temporal increase in coupling strength in the simulation, allowing it to double by ~15 ss, led to a decrease in the time to FRS that reproduced the experimental results.
claims.source: A temporal increase in coupling strength in the simulation, allowing it to double by ~15 ss, led to a decrease in the time to FRS that reproduced the experimental results, Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations that matches experimental data, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claims.claim: The increase in the coupling strength over somite stages alone is sufficient to realize the dependence of time to FRS on twash-out.
claims.source: These results indicate that the increase in the coupling strength over somite stages alone is sufficient to realize the dependence of time to FRS on twash-out, whereas the global tissue parameters contribute to the behavior of PLD observed in experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from simulation results.

claims.claim: The model with all three effects combined (PSM shortening, change in cell advection pattern, and increase in coupling strength) quantitatively reproduced the behaviors of FRS and PLD.
claims.source: The requirement for many realizations to compute FRS and PLD precluded application of standard fitting procedures for determining parameter values in the model. Instead, we used parameter values close to those observed in embryos. We found a decrease in time to PLD with the magnitude of the decrease greater than time to FRS, as observed in the experimental data, Figure 4E.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations that matches experimental data, illustrated in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Inclusion of the PSM shortening and change in cell advection pattern in simulations recapitulated the experimental observation that the difference between PLD and FRS became smaller with later washout time.
claims.source: Inclusion of the PSM shortening and change in cell advection pattern in simulations recapitulated the experimental observation that the difference between PLD and FRS became smaller with later washout time.
claims.evidence: This is a result from simulations that matches experimental data.

claims.claim: A change in the coupling strength was sufficient to reproduce the behavior of FRS.
claims.source: In summary, a change in the coupling strength was sufficient to reproduce the behavior of FRS.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claims.claim: Combined effects of the PSM shortening and cell advection pattern were the dominant factors that generated the behaviors of PLD in simulations.
claims.source: Combined effects of the PSM shortening and cell advection pattern were the dominant factors that generated the behaviors of PLD in simulations.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claims.claim: The physical model quantitatively reproduced the behaviors of FRS and PLD, suggesting that the physiologically plausible changes in these tissue parameters may underlie behaviors observed in the experiment.

results.result: Delta-Notch signaling is required for local synchronization between neighboring cells in the vertebrate segmentation clock, and its inhibition causes defective segment boundaries. This is supported by established knowledge and prior experimental work showing desynchronization in Delta-Notch mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C8-C15 collectively establish the role of Delta-Notch signaling in the segmentation clock based on extensive prior work. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. The mechanistic details (C8-C10) and phenotypic observations (C11-C15) are consistent with the broader claim.

results.result: The desynchronization hypothesis postulates a critical synchrony threshold (Zc) below which defective segments form, and this theory quantitatively explains the anterior limit of defects in Delta-Notch mutants. DAPT can be used to inhibit and then restore Delta-Notch signaling, allowing resynchronization.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C24 describe the theoretical framework (desynchronization hypothesis) and experimental tool (DAPT) that form the foundation of this study. These are well-supported by citations to prior work (C19, C21-C24) and represent established concepts. The claims are internally consistent and provide the necessary background for the current work.

results.result: Early DAPT washout at 9.5 hpf causes intermingling of normal and defective segments, a phenotype not anticipated by previous models. This suggests persistent fluctuations in synchrony level near the critical threshold Zc.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C43-C44 report a key experimental observation illustrated in Figure 1G,I. The intermingling phenotype is clearly documented and represents a novel finding. C26 appropriately contextualizes this as unexpected based on prior models. The interpretation (C44) is reasonable given the data, though it remains an inference that the model will later address.

results.result: The experimental protocol involved DAPT administration at 4 hpf for at least 5 hours, with segment patterns visualized by xirp2a in situ hybridization at ~36 hpf. Defects were scored and quantified using defined metrics (ALD, FRS, PLD).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C37 describe the experimental methodology in detail. The protocol is clearly described (C27-C29), defect types are illustrated (C30), and the quantification metrics are well-defined (C31-C37). The definition of FRS after segment 9 (C37) is justified by the observation that desynchronization continues until that point (C36). These methodological claims are internally consistent and adequately documented.

results.result: With late DAPT washout at 14 hpf, embryos formed several defective segments followed by recovery of normal segments, with PLD coinciding closely with FRS. This pattern is consistent with monotonic increase in synchrony after crossing the threshold Zc.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 describe the late washout phenotype illustrated in Figure 1C,H. The observations are clearly documented and the interpretation (C42) is consistent with the desynchronization hypothesis. The close coincidence of PLD and FRS (C41) supports the inference of monotonic synchrony increase. These claims are well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: A physical model of the PSM and tailbud was developed describing cells as particles in a U-shaped 3D domain, subject to physical forces, intrinsic mobility gradients, cell advection, and a frequency profile that generates kinematic phase waves.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C54 describe the physical model framework illustrated in Figure 2. The model components are clearly defined and based on prior experimental observations (C47-C49 cite previous work). The model successfully generates kinematic phase waves from synchronized initial conditions (C51), demonstrating internal consistency. The model description is comprehensive and well-documented in the Materials and methods.

results.result: Resynchronization simulations starting from random phases show spatially heterogeneous recovery with formation of persistent phase vortices that are advected to the anterior PSM, causing intermingled defects. The defect size distribution matches experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C70 describe the core simulation results illustrated in Figure 3. The model qualitatively reproduces the intermingling phenotype (C57, C64) through vortex formation and advection (C65-C67). Importantly, the defect size distributions quantitatively match experimental data (C69), providing strong validation. The vorticity analysis (C66) provides mechanistic insight. These claims are well-supported by the simulation data and experimental comparison.

results.result: Systematic parameter analysis reveals that FRS is determined by parameters affecting local synchronization (coupling strength, PSM radius), while PLD is additionally influenced by parameters controlling vortex transport (PSM length, cell advection pattern, cell mixing).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C84 describe comprehensive parameter sensitivity analysis illustrated in Figure 3 supplements 4-11. The systematic variation of individual parameters and their differential effects on FRS vs PLD are clearly documented. The mechanistic explanations (C72-C75, C78, C80) are consistent with the model structure. The summary conclusions (C83-C84) appropriately synthesize the findings. This analysis is thorough and well-supported.

results.result: Simulations incorporating PSM shortening and changing advection patterns predict that PSM shortening decreases time to PLD for later washouts without affecting FRS, while changes in advection pattern increase time to PLD for earlier washouts, also without affecting FRS.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 describe predictions from simulations with time-varying tissue parameters, illustrated in Figure 4B-C and supplements. The differential effects on PLD vs FRS are clearly demonstrated and mechanistically explained (C85, C88). The prediction (C90) follows logically from the simulation results. These claims are well-supported by the simulation data.

results.result: Experimental DAPT washout at different developmental times shows that both FRS and PLD increase with later washout, time to PLD decreases over development as predicted, but time to FRS also decreases unexpectedly, with more scattered defects at earlier washouts.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 report experimental observations from Figure 4D-E and supplements. The data clearly show the developmental trends in FRS and PLD (C91-C92). The discrepancy between observed and predicted FRS behavior (C93) is honestly reported and motivates further model development. The observations are well-documented and internally consistent.

results.result: To explain the unexpected decrease in time to FRS with developmental stage, the model was extended to include temporally increasing coupling strength, which successfully reproduced the experimental FRS behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 describe the hypothesis and test of increasing coupling strength, illustrated in Figure 4 supplement 5. The hypothesis (C96-C97) is reasonable given the discrepancy with prior simulations. The simulation with increasing coupling (C98) successfully reproduces the experimental trend. The conclusion (C99) appropriately summarizes the finding. However, the coupling strength increase remains an assumption that would benefit from direct experimental validation in future work.

results.result: The complete model combining PSM shortening, changing advection pattern, and increasing coupling strength quantitatively reproduces both FRS and PLD behaviors observed experimentally, with coupling strength dominating FRS and tissue parameters dominating PLD.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 describe the final integrated model results shown in Figure 4E. The model successfully captures the experimental trends in both FRS and PLD (C100-C101). The mechanistic attribution (C102-C103) is consistent with the parameter analysis. The conclusion (C104) appropriately summarizes the achievement while noting the parameters are 'physiologically plausible' rather than directly measured. The quantitative agreement is impressive given model complexity.

results.result: The spatial distribution of segment defects along the axis is predicted by the model and matches experimental observations, with left-right independence of recovery confirmed by probabilistic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 describe validation of the model against the spatial defect distribution, illustrated in Figure 4F and supplements 7-8. The agreement between simulation and experiment (C107) provides additional validation beyond FRS/PLD. The left-right independence analysis (C108) adds rigor. The summary (C109) appropriately characterizes the model's predictive capability. These claims are well-supported by the data.

results.result: Segmental pattern recovery after DAPT washout occurs at two scales: rapid local synchronization between neighboring cells and slower transport of patterns through tissue morphogenesis, with intermingled segments explained by advection of persistent phase vortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 state the main conclusions of the study. The experimental observation of intermingling (C4) is well-documented. The theoretical explanation via vortices (C5) is supported by simulations. The predictions about tissue parameters (C6) are validated experimentally. The two-scale conclusion (C7) appropriately synthesizes the findings. These high-level claims are well-supported by the detailed results, though the vortices themselves remain to be directly observed experimentally.
